finding.claim: The /settings/email POST route uses @login_optional instead of @login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach set_email with g.uid=None. This is a missing authentication check on a state-changing, account-modifying operation. It enables account-takeover primitives, such as changing the email of a null or unassigned user record, or of whatever record uid None maps to. The sibling /settings/password route correctly uses @login_required, which indicates this is a departure from the pattern. Also note that there is no CSRF protection on the POST endpoints.
finding.source: Any unauthenticated remote client sending POST /settings/email with no session cookie
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, which modifies account email

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid'), which is None when unauthenticated, and never aborts
set_email(None, ...) is called without any authentication check

finding.guards_checked: login_required (not used on this route); login_optional does not enforce auth; no other checks in the handler; no CSRF protection. set_email is a stub, so the real impact depends on its implementation, but the missing auth gate is present on the route itself.

verdict.guard_found: none (login_optional at routes.py:19-25 only sets g.uid and never aborts; no check in change_email)
verdict.reason: routes.py:34-37 exposes POST /settings/email behind @login_optional (routes.py:22 sets g.uid=None, no abort), so anonymous callers reach set_email(None, ...), unlike /settings/password's @login_required (routes.py:42); set_email is a stub (routes.py:48-49) so real impact depends on its implementation, and the email is hardcoded.
